# The 4am toast

My last night shift was on Saturday 7 November 2026: nine at night until half past seven the next morning, in majors. After fourteen years of nights, I expected the ending to feel more definite. A last something. Instead, it was a shift, and then it was over.

I did my first night as an SHO in 2012. On Monday, I start a days-only rota. This is a sensible change, made for sensible reasons. My knees have had enough. My sleep has become something I negotiate with rather than something I reliably get. My GP has also made it clear that my blood pressure is not a joke any more.

All of that is straightforward. What has surprised me is how not-okay I feel about the rest of it.

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers around, less ceremony, and fewer opportunities for anyone to pretend they are having a better shift than they are. People are more honest at three in the morning. Often, they are kinder too.

This is not because night staff are special. It is difficult to maintain much of a performance when you have been awake for too long and someone has just asked you the same reasonable question for the fourth time. You either find a little more patience or you discover that you haven’t got any. Either way, the night finds out.

At four, someone makes toast in the staff room.

Not every single night, perhaps, but often enough that it counts as a law of the department. Nobody admits to starting it. There is no rota and, as far as I know, no toaster ownership dispute. You simply reach the part of the shift when the night has stopped being new and morning is still an insultingly distant idea, and the smell of toast appears.

It is never ceremonial. Someone eats a slice standing up. Someone else says they don’t want any and then takes one. Occasionally there is a brief, serious conversation about why toast made by somebody else is better than toast made at home. Then everybody goes back to work.

I am going to miss that more than seems reasonable.

People think nights are about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. Mostly, though, they are about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

Not heroic kindness. Just explaining something again without putting an edge on your voice. Noticing that someone is frightened before they have worked out how to tell you. Making tea for a colleague who has gone quiet. Sitting down for thirty seconds when standing over somebody would make the whole interaction feel different.

Nights taught me that kindness is not always a feeling. Quite often it is a practice, performed with limited resources by people who are also cold, hungry and desperate for the toilet.

I hope I can take that into the daylight.

They gave me other things too: friends I would not have chosen in advance and now cannot imagine doing without; a confidence that arrived slowly and without much drama; the discovery that people can be extremely funny while also completely exhausted. Folasade, our charge nurse, has done nights for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. This has been going on for long enough that I have stopped pretending I am letting her win.

But nights took things as well, and I don’t want to write about them as though they were just a difficult but wonderful adventure.

In my first winter of nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I could not remember whether I had given a second dose. I had given it. There had been no mistake. I was simply so tired that my mind had started presenting ordinary uncertainties as emergencies.

I remember sitting there with no idea how to make myself go home. I also remember the frost on the windscreen. It is strange what survives: not the whole shift, not even the Fear with its original force, but the pattern of ice on glass and the absolute conviction that I was not fit to be trusted with anything.

I do not miss that version of myself.

Nights also take the parts of life that do not look dramatic when you type them into a rota request. Both my nieces’ naming ceremonies happened while nights kept me elsewhere. I joined over video, which was better than not being there, but it was not being there.

My sister never once complained. She never made me feel that I had chosen badly or loved anybody less. She simply kept finding ways to include me. Only now am I properly understanding how generous that was, and how easy it would have been for her to be less gracious about it.

There is no useful lesson in this except that video calls are not the same as a room full of people, and that the people who love you can shield you from the cost of your choices for a very long time.

Still, some of the moments I will keep are so small that I could not have predicted them.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an elderly gentleman held my hand and told me that I had his daughter’s hands. He went home three days later. There is no hidden twist to the story, and I don’t want to turn it into one. It was simply an unexpected kindness at an hour when I did not feel especially full of anything worth giving.

At night, care does not always travel in the direction written on the paperwork.

After my last shift, I drove home down London Road. The sun was coming up and I had the Radio 4 shipping forecast on catch-up, which is either a very fitting soundtrack or evidence that I should never be allowed to curate a significant moment.

I have driven home in that light hundreds of times. Usually I have been thinking about sleep, food, or whether I had remembered to do something ordinary before leaving. This time I realised that I would not see that light from that side again.

I will see other sunrises. I may even start seeing them voluntarily, although let us not make commitments this early in the new rota. But there is a particular morning light that belongs to the drive home after nights. Everything looks slightly overexposed. Other people are beginning their day while you are carrying the whole of yours behind your eyes. You are relieved to be leaving and vaguely offended that the world has continued without noticing what time it is for you.

And I am relieved. That is the other thing I have not quite known what to do with.

I am relieved about sleep. Relieved about my knees. Relieved that my GP may soon have one less thing to say in that tone. Relieved at the thought of occasionally eating dinner with other people and then going to bed at the same time as them.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved.

It feels disloyal to the people still doing the next night, and the one after that. It feels disloyal to the person who cried in the car park and then came back. Somewhere along the way, endurance became tangled up with virtue, and now stopping feels as if I am rewriting the story to make myself the person who escaped.

But I have wanted this change, and I am sad about it. Both things are true. Neither cancels out the other, however inconvenient that is for someone trying to write a tidy ending.

So I will leave the tidy ending alone.

Folasade will probably still beat everybody up the stairs. At four, someone will put the toast on. A few people will wander into the staff room and then wander out again. Nobody will admit to starting it, and nobody will make a speech about it.

That seems like enough to be going on with.
